title: Dynamic behavior of the buck power stage

lessons.title: Energy exchange, resonance, and damping
lessons.physicalIntuition: The inductor and capacitor can exchange energy; resistance and load remove it. A lighter resistive load removes less energy per oscillation and can increase plant peaking.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Linearize the averaged buck state equations and identify the second-order denominator, natural frequency near 1/sqrt(LC), damping terms that include load and parasitics, and the ESR numerator zero.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The pole-zero explorer recalculates the plant at the selected load and nonidealities. It must not reuse a full-load plant at no load without disclosure.
assumptions: small perturbation about a periodic CCM operating point
lessons.transferQuestion: At fixed L and C, predict the Bode peaking change as resistive load increases by 10×.

lessons.title: Three disturbance paths
lessons.physicalIntuition: A control command, input-line movement, and load-current disturbance enter the converter through different physical paths, so one phrase such as 'buck bandwidth' cannot identify all responses.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Perturb duty/control, input voltage, and load current independently in the linearized state equations to obtain Gvd, Gvg, and Zout with other independent inputs set to zero as specified.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Every analysis panel names excitation and measured output. Replace 'power-stage bandwidth' with LC resonance, a named plant transfer-function feature, or a defined time response.
assumptions: superposition applies only to the linearized model
lessons.transferQuestion: Which response predicts initial sensitivity to a small load-current perturbation and what sign convention does it use?

lessons.title: Averaged versus switched models
lessons.physicalIntuition: Averaging keeps slow energy motion but erases the pulse train. Linearization additionally keeps only small deviations around one mode and operating point.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Weight state equations by duty for an averaged CCM model, then write x = X + x-hat and discard products of perturbations. In DCM an extra interval/constraint changes the averaged model. Sampling effects become important near switching-related frequencies.
lessons.modelingConsequence: Never use an averaged result to display jitter, pulse skipping, dead-time current paths, phase collision, or switch-node voltage. Mark AC plots with operating mode and conservative validity limits.
lessons.transferQuestion: Why can the averaged output response be useful while its switch-node trace would be meaningless?
